q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE system of servitude practiced between 1450 and 1750.
parts.b: Explain ONE reason why European colonists turned to African chattel slavery rather than other forms of labor, using the historian's interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE difference between chattel slavery in the Americas and indentured servitude.

sample_answers.a: The Spanish encomienda granted colonists the right to extract labor and tribute from indigenous communities, theoretically in exchange for Christian instruction — a system that devastated native populations through overwork and disease.
sample_answers.b: According to the passage, enslaved Africans were preferred because they could be worked for life and their children enslaved in turn, because their dark skin made escape and rebellion harder in societies organized by race, and because European traders had already built the infrastructure to supply them.
sample_answers.c: Chattel slavery was lifelong, hereditary, and racial — enslaved people were legal property with no rights — while indentured servants worked for a fixed term (typically 4–7 years) under a contract and regained freedom afterward.

q1.stimulus:
Historians distinguish several systems of coerced labor in the early modern world, but none matched the scale or brutality of transatlantic chattel slavery. The Spanish used the encomienda to exploit indigenous labor; the English sent indentured servants who worked fixed terms for passage to America; the Russians bound peasants as serfs. Yet by 1700, plantation colonies from Brazil to Virginia depended overwhelmingly on enslaved Africans. Historians explain this shift as the result of intersecting factors: indigenous populations had been devastated by disease, indentured servants could run away and blend into free society, and European merchants had already created the trading networks to deliver captive Africans. Most fatefully, colonists racialized slavery — defining it as the permanent, hereditary condition of Africans — which allowed them to reconcile bondage with emerging ideas of liberty for Europeans.
—Historian's account of systems of servitude in the period c. 1450–1750

q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE condition of the Middle Passage described by Equiano.
parts.b: Describe ONE way in which Equiano's account challenges justifications of the slave trade.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why Equiano's narrative was powerful evidence for the abolitionist movement.

sample_answers.a: Equiano describes enslaved people packed so tightly below deck that they could barely move, surrounded by filth and stench, with the sick and dying chained among the living.
sample_answers.b: Defenders of slavery claimed Africans were well-treated cargo; Equiano's firsthand testimony of suffocation, disease, and despair exposed the trade's systematic cruelty and the humanity of its victims.
sample_answers.c: As a formerly enslaved African who had purchased his freedom and learned to write, Equiano embodied the abolitionists' argument that Africans were fully human and capable — his own life refuted the racism that justified slavery.

q2.stimulus:
The stench of the hold while we were on the coast was so intolerably loathsome that it was dangerous to remain there for any time, and some of us had been permitted to stay on the deck for the fresh air; but now that the whole ship's cargo were confined together, it became absolutely pestilential. The closeness of the place, and the heat of the climate, added to the number in the ship, which was so crowded that each had scarcely room to turn himself, almost suffocated us. This wretched situation was again aggravated by the galling of the chains, now become insupportable, and the filth of the necessary tubs, into which the children often fell, and were almost suffocated.
—Olaudah Equiano, The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, 1789

q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE feature of the diagram that illustrates the conditions of the Middle Passage.
parts.b: Explain ONE purpose for which British abolitionists used this diagram.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which the diagram's portrayal of enslaved Africans as passive victims was both effective and limiting.

sample_answers.a: The diagram shows hundreds of human figures packed in neat rows into every deck of the ship, with each person allocated a space barely wider than their body — visualizing human beings stowed like cargo.
sample_answers.b: Abolitionists circulated the diagram widely to make the abstract horror of the slave trade concrete: viewers could see at a glance the systematic, calculated cruelty of packing 400+ people into a ship's hold.
sample_answers.c: The image was effective because its cold, technical precision made the inhumanity undeniable; but it was limiting because it showed Africans only as suffering bodies, not as people who resisted — through revolts, suicides, and sabotage — or as agents in their own liberation.

q3.stimulus: The image is the famous 1789 diagram of the British slave ship Brookes, published by abolitionists to show how enslaved Africans were packed into the ship's holds for the Middle Passage. The engraving depicts 454 enslaved men, women, and children (the legal limit under the 1788 Slave Trade Act) arranged in tight rows on multiple decks — though the ship had actually carried as many as 740. The diagram became one of the most powerful visual weapons of the abolitionist movement.
